Descriptives and regression

Source: vignettes/articles/descriptives-models.Rmd
descriptives-models.Rmd

Prepare one survey design

Declare the cohort in nis_design() and keep the columns needed by the summary and model.

nis <- nis_open(nis_example(years = 2019:2020)) |>
  nis_flag_dx(heart_failure = "I50") |>
  dplyr::mutate(death = as.integer(DIED))

design <- nis_design(
  nis,
  cohort = AGE >= 18,
  keep = c(AGE, FEMALE, LOS, DIED, death, heart_failure),
  annualize = TRUE
)
#> Warning: Missing values are always removed in SQL aggregation functions.
#> Use `na.rm = TRUE` to silence this warning
#> This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
#> Cohort: 192 discharges; weighted N 114.4; 24 hospitals across 2 years.

The design contains adult cohort rows. For hospital-years with no cohort rows, nis_design() adds placeholder rows so those hospital-years remain represented in the design’s variance structure. This placeholder method is experimental; review the design construction and its suitability for your analysis.

Estimate weighted summaries

srvyr adds tidy verbs to survey designs. The total below is an annualized weighted discharge estimate; the mean and its standard error use the survey design.

srvyr::summarise(
  design,
  discharges = srvyr::survey_total(),
  mean_age = srvyr::survey_mean(AGE),
  death_rate = srvyr::survey_mean(death)
)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   discharges discharges_se mean_age mean_age_se death_rate death_rate_se
#>        <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>      <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1       114.          2.83     59.6       0.597     0.0201       0.00829

All values come from invented rows and illustrate output shape only.

Build a Table 1

gtsummary::tbl_svysummary() formats weighted descriptive statistics. These optional packages are needed for this section.

table_one <- gtsummary::tbl_svysummary(
  design,
  by = heart_failure,
  include = c(AGE, FEMALE, LOS, DIED)
) |>
  gtsummary::add_overall()
table_one

The columns compare the flag groups with an overall column. Inspect the unweighted cell counts before sharing; the table is not automatically disclosure-cleared.

Fit a survey-weighted model

survey::svyglm() fits generalized linear models using the design.

fit <- survey::svyglm(
  death ~ heart_failure + AGE + FEMALE + factor(YEAR),
  design = design,
  family = quasibinomial()
)
summary(fit)
#> 
#> Call:
#> svyglm(formula = death ~ heart_failure + AGE + FEMALE + factor(YEAR), 
#>     design = design, family = quasibinomial())
#> 
#> Survey design:
#> Called via srvyr
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)       1.639e+00  1.906e+00   0.860  0.40442    
#> heart_failureYes -8.726e-01  1.715e+00  -0.509  0.61872    
#> AGE              -9.999e-02  2.814e-02  -3.553  0.00318 ** 
#> FEMALEFemale     -1.836e+01  7.455e-01 -24.626  6.3e-13 ***
#> factor(YEAR)2020 -3.784e-16  8.742e-01   0.000  1.00000    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> (Dispersion parameter for quasibinomial family taken to be 0.1660637)
#> 
#> Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 20

Coefficients describe model associations under the survey design; they do not establish causality. The synthetic data are too small and artificial for substantive conclusions.

Common pitfalls

Common pitfalls

  • Use survey/srvyr methods on the survey design, not ordinary row-level summaries when reporting design-based uncertainty.
  • A weighted estimate does not validate the cohort definition, model, or causal interpretation.
  • Apply disclosure review separately; weighted summaries alone do not show whether counts are safe to report.

See Survey design and weighting, nis_design(), and Disclosure and suppression.
